video_title: Hollywood Was Cooked Before AI, and Now It's Only Getting Worse | Odd Lots
gist: Former Family Guy/Eastbound and Down writer and ex-LA City Hall staffer Hayes Davenport, live with Odd Lots' Tracy Alloway and Joe Weisenthal, argues Hollywood's decline predates AI: LA shoot days have halved from ~40,000 in 2016 to under 20,000, driven by the cable-to-streaming shift, the pandemic, the 2023 strikes and tax-break-driven runaway production. Writers' rooms have shrunk toward single-writer models, library content competes with new shows, and AI now threatens below-the-line production jobs, with knock-on effects for LA restaurants, studio real estate, tourism and nightlife.

insights.claim: Los Angeles film/TV shoot days peaked at about 40,000 in 2016, leveled to ~37,000 by 2019, recovered after the pandemic to 2019 levels in 2022, then fell to ~25,000 after the 2023 strikes, ~23,000 the next year, and under 20,000 despite the industry mantra 'survive till 25' — roughly half the 2016 level.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: LA production volume is in structural, not cyclical, decline — a leading indicator for LA-exposed studio real estate, production services and local economy.
insights.quote: the mantra I think a lot of people heard in the city was survive till 25.

insights.claim: The 2016–2019 dip in LA shoot days reflected streaming (Netflix, Amazon, new networks) growing while network and cable production shrank — e.g., Comedy Central largely stopped making new shows.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: Streaming did not fully replace lost cable/network volume even at its peak spending phase — the content pie shrank as distribution shifted.

insights.claim: Writers Guild membership swelled in the late 2010s as cable veterans remained members while new streaming shows brought in newcomers; with production since cut in half, those newer writers are losing opportunities, many moving home or taking survival jobs.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: An oversupplied creative labor pool facing halved demand implies continued wage pressure and weak bargaining leverage for writers.

insights.claim: US production has been a state-by-state 'race to the bottom' on tax incentives: Eastbound and Down left North Carolina when the governor ended its tax break, and the same team moved to South Carolina for Vice Principals and Righteous Gemstones.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: Production is highly mobile and follows incentives; state tax-credit changes directly move production spending and local jobs.
insights.quote: It follows the Great show, the tax break, great show.

insights.claim: Even studio-bound formats are leaving LA: Fox game shows and studio comedies are being shot in Dublin, Ireland, and many productions shoot in Vancouver, for tax and labor-cost reasons; Netflix is building a $1 billion studio in New Jersey.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: Offshoring of even low-complexity formats signals LA's cost disadvantage is broad-based, not limited to location shoots.

insights.claim: Studio space in LA financed around the 2016 production peak — including a giant complex near Santa Monica Boulevard and the 101 that broke ground around 2019 — is now completed into weak demand, causing issues in LA studio real estate.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: LA soundstage owners and lenders face an oversupply built on peak-cycle assumptions — a credit/occupancy risk to watch.

insights.claim: TV writing is shifting to the cheaper single-writer 'Mike White model' (The White Lotus), which studios prefer; comedies like Great News once had 30 writers, a staffing level Davenport says will never exist again, and seven writers now counts as a big room.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: Labor cost per episode is being structurally cut on the creative side — margin-supportive for studios, deflationary for writer employment.
insights.quote: I had 30 writers when I was there. That does not exist any more and never, ever will again.

insights.claim: Post-strike WGA rules that require a triggered writers' room to be a minimum size for a minimum number of weeks have pushed studios toward avoiding rooms altogether — e.g., a show where creators hired one person to outline the season for a couple of weeks and then wrote it themselves.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: Union minimums can backfire into fewer rooms — an example of labor protections accelerating substitution.

insights.claim: New TV shows now compete against the entire back library (e.g., Family Guy) rather than just what's airing on rival networks; top individual titles like Family Guy and The Office still command big prices, but large chunks of libraries are becoming less valuable.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: Library value is bifurcating — marquee franchises hold pricing power while long-tail catalog gets commoditized, relevant to valuing media-asset sales.
insights.quote: The entire library, is is competition not just what's on the other network at the same time.

insights.claim: Scripted entertainment has for years competed against 'the sum of all human creativity' distributed free and algorithmically sorted, so AI content is less of a new threat — and AI is cheaper but 'not as cheap as free', with consumption hours as the binding constraint.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: The real competitor for attention is free user-generated content; AI's marginal disruption to demand may be smaller than to production costs.
insights.quote: We have already been competing for years against the sum of all human creativity. Produced and distributed for free. Yes. Algorithmically sorted exactly to your specifications. You can't really scare us.

insights.claim: Horror is the most alive film genre because mid-budget horror, pioneered by Blumhouse (Paranormal Activity), has commercial upside that studios will greenlight, pulling comedy talent like Zach Cregger and Jordan Peele into horror while comedy productions decline.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: Capital is flowing to genres with asymmetric theatrical upside; low-budget horror IP remains the studio sweet spot while comedy gets squeezed.

insights.claim: Short stories — including Reddit posts and unpublished pieces by anonymous writers — have become popular IP for studios to acquire, with it hard to tell whether some were written by AI.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: Studios are sourcing cheap, low-provenance IP — a channel where AI-generated material may quietly enter the pipeline.

insights.claim: Los Angeles is among the least generative-AI-friendly cities, with strong stigma against AI use in productions because it threatens 'below-the-line' production jobs — hair and makeup, set design, grips — which Davenport says are on an immediate precipice.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: AI substitution risk is most acute for production crew rather than writers; cultural and union resistance is a friction slowing studio adoption.

insights.claim: Studios have not yet replaced writers' rooms with AI despite new WGA contract AI guardrails, because comedy is the hardest genre for AI; but AI can already do outlines and other genres more easily, and Davenport says the capability is 'right there', not distant.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: Expect AI to enter via outlines and non-comedy genres first; union guardrails are unenforceable at home, limiting their protective value.
insights.quote: it's not in like the distant future that it'll be able to do that stuff

insights.claim: Davenport believes writing and acting will be among the last categories AI can do well, and Joe Weisenthal reports AI models still fail to convincingly imitate his tweeting voice.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport; Joe Weisenthal (host)
insights.so_what: Voice- and humor-driven creative work remains a relative moat for now, though the speaker admits this may be naive.

insights.claim: Hollywood is roughly 20% of the LA economy but tightly linked to it: restaurants weakened by the pandemic shutdown were pushed over the edge by the production decline, since productions and writers' rooms buy large volumes of catered meals from local businesses.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: Production declines have multiplier effects on LA small business, consumer spending and municipal tax receipts.

insights.claim: LA has lost its role as the exporter of lifestyle culture to social-media-native New York; the influencer economy brings subscriber money into LA (e.g., global awareness of Erewhon smoothies) but LA 'doesn't own it' as it did screen culture, and nightlife has shifted to a 'DoorDash' stay-home culture.
insights.speaker: Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: The creator economy partially offsets studio decline but is geographically diffuse, weakening LA's tourism and nightlife pull.
insights.quote: There's a real DoorDash nightlife culture.

insights.claim: The monoculture that produced universally known movie stars has ended; few new stars on the scale of George Clooney have emerged, and LA celebrities are now less publicly visible.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal (host); Hayes Davenport
insights.so_what: Fragmented attention reduces the star-power moat that underpinned theatrical economics and tourism.
